intro: Iwata maps one tree: Yuya no Naga Fuji, a wisteria at Gyokoji Temple whose kanji name is usually read Kumano but is read locally as Yuya, after a court lady from the centuries-old Noh play named for her. Legend says she planted the vine herself in the late Heian period. It has held National Natural Monument status since 1932 and is the centre of an annual spring festival. Published alone here because the tree itself is the destination, not because Iwata's research is finished.

question_context: The vine grows on the grounds of Gyokoji Temple in Ikeda, reached by bus or taxi from JR Iwata or Fukude station, since no rail line reaches the temple directly. Free to visit; the city runs an annual wisteria festival with night illumination and temporary parking during the mid-to-late April bloom. Its kanji name is usually read Kumano, but is read locally as Yuya, after Yuya Gozen, a court lady from the Noh play named for her, who local legend says planted the vine herself before leaving for Kyoto in the late Heian period. Its trellis has grown from roughly 400 square metres in 1907 to about 1,600 today, and its flower clusters typically reach over a metre long, with a recorded maximum of 1.5 metres. Five younger wisterias on the same temple grounds carry their own separate designation, each roughly 250 years old, but this is the vine the temple, the town and the festival are named for.

trees.story:
The kanji in this wisteria's name is usually read Kumano. Here, at Gyokoji Temple in Iwata, it is read Yuya instead, after Yuya Gozen, a court lady from a centuries-old Noh play named for her. Local legend holds she planted this vine herself in the late Heian period before leaving for Kyoto, and the reading has stuck for as long as anyone has written the tree down. It is not a mistake to correct.

What has grown from that planting is now judged around 800 to 850 years old and covers a trellis that has expanded from roughly 400 square metres in 1907 to about 1,600 today, folding in the neighbouring memorial park as it spread. Its flower clusters typically reach over a metre long, with a recorded maximum of 1.5 metres and older reports of clusters twice that. Five younger wisterias on the same temple grounds carry their own separate designation, each roughly 250 years old, but this is the one the temple, the town and the festival are named for.

Iwata has run an annual wisteria festival around the vine for as long as anyone has logged the date, with night illumination extending viewing hours through the mid-to-late April bloom. It has held National Natural Monument status since 1932. A wisteria old enough to outlive the play written about the woman who planted it is a tree people build a spring trip around, not one they pass without noticing.
